title: Ingress & Network Policies
intro: A ClusterIP Service isn't reachable from outside the cluster. Ingress handles external HTTP(S) routing; NetworkPolicies control which pods can talk to which.

steps.prompt: List the Ingress resources in the namespace.
steps.fake_output:
NAME      CLASS   HOSTS              ADDRESS        PORTS   AGE
web-ing   nginx   web.example.com    203.0.113.10   80      1h
steps.explanation: An Ingress routes external HTTP traffic (by hostname/path) to internal Services — it's how 'web.example.com' actually reaches the 'web' Service.
steps.why: A LoadBalancer Service could also expose something externally, but that's one IP per Service. Ingress lets many hostnames/paths share a single external IP and load balancer.

steps.prompt: Get the full routing details of the 'web-ing' Ingress.
steps.fake_output:
Name: web-ing
Host: web.example.com
Path: /
Backend: web:80
Annotations: kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
steps.explanation: This confirms exactly which Service and port the hostname/path is wired to.
steps.why: 'kubectl get ingress web-ing -o yaml' shows the same rules, but describe is faster to read when you just need to confirm the backend Service and port.

steps.prompt: Check if there are any NetworkPolicies restricting traffic in this namespace.
steps.explanation: If a pod suddenly can't reach another pod it could reach yesterday, a NetworkPolicy — not a Service or DNS issue — is a common, easy-to-miss cause.
steps.why: There's no NetworkPolicy equivalent of 'describe pod' style troubleshooting on the receiving end — you have to explicitly check for policies, since by default all traffic is allowed unless one exists.

steps.prompt: Get the details of the 'deny-from-other' policy to see exactly what it blocks.
steps.fake_output:
Name: deny-from-other
Pod Selector: app=db
Allowing ingress traffic:
  From: PodSelector app=web
Policy Types: Ingress
steps.explanation: This policy means: pods labeled app=db only accept incoming traffic from pods labeled app=web — everything else is dropped.
steps.why: NetworkPolicies are allow-lists, not block-lists — once any policy selects a pod, everything not explicitly allowed is denied, which is why 'nothing matches' silently breaks things instead of erroring.
